summary:
The Preventing the Financing of Illegal Synthetic Drugs Act (Pub. L. 118-79, H.R. 1076), enacted September 13, 2024, is a freestanding directive statute that mandates a Government Accountability Office study on illicit financing connected to synthetic drug trafficking. It does not amend the U.S. Code, create any new substantive authority, impose regulatory obligations, or authorize or appropriate funds.

Section 1 provides the short title. Section 2 sets forth congressional findings, citing CDC overdose mortality data, UNODC statistics on the proliferation of New Psychoactive Substances, and congressional testimony regarding fentanyl trafficking economics and the role of illicit finance in sustaining organized crime networks.

Section 3 is the sole operative provision. Subsection (a) directs the Comptroller General of the United States to carry out a study on illicit financing in connection with the trafficking of synthetic drugs—expressly including fentanyl and methamphetamine, fentanyl- and methamphetamine-related substances, Captagon, and fentanyl and methamphetamine precursors. The study must address seven enumerated subjects: (1) the trafficking business and related illicit finance, including participation of transnational criminal organizations and terror syndicates and notable trafficking corridors (source and transit countries); (2) the organizations' business models across precursor purchase/production, supply-chain movement, manufacture, marketing, distribution, sales, and return of proceeds; (3) the overlap between human-trafficking and synthetic-drug-trafficking business models; (4) use of online illicit drug markets and social media for marketing, sale, and payment; (5) financial methods, including payment, money laundering, and repatriation of proceeds; (6) use of specified social media applications (Snapchat, Discord, Facebook) and payment applications (CashApp) to facilitate transactions, particularly among young people; and (7) U.S. Government activities to combat related illicit finance, including interagency, intergovernmental, and intersectoral (private-sector) collaboration under subparagraphs (A)–(C), and identified gaps or resource deficiencies in those coordination and collaboration activities (subparagraph (D)).

Subsection (b) imposes a reporting deadline: not later than the end of the one-year period beginning on the date of enactment, the Comptroller General must issue a report to Congress containing all findings and determinations made in carrying out the study.

The Act contains no severability clause, sunset provision, effective-date provision (other than the report deadline), or enforcement mechanism. Its legal effect is limited to the study-and-report mandate directed at the Comptroller General.
